title: Core Strength
subtitle: Build a trunk that supports lifting, carrying, balance, and everyday movement

blocks.text: This lesson is general education, not diagnosis, treatment or rehab. Fill out CSEP’s Get Active Questionnaire before a big increase in activity and follow what it says. Get qualified advice for recent belly, pelvic, spine or hip surgery; pregnancy or postpartum concerns; a hernia; osteoporosis; back or pelvic pain that won’t go away; weakness or numbness you can’t explain; or a condition that changes how you exercise. Stop and get urgent medical help for chest pressure or pain, fainting, severe or unusual shortness of breath, sudden nerve symptoms, losing control of your bladder or bowels, or severe pain after a fall.

You’ll test how your trunk supports five everyday jobs: breathing, resisting unwanted movement, passing force between your upper and lower body, carrying and changing position. No heroic plank face required. Your eyebrows may stay relaxed.
Carry, lift and move with more control in everyday life.
blocks.detail: A core trained for real tasks makes groceries, stairs and lifting feel steadier, not just your plank time longer.
blocks.extra: Section 05 shows how to train your trunk in more than one direction.

sections.title: Give the Core a Real Job

blocks.text: Your core includes the muscles around your belly, sides, back, pelvis, hips and breathing. These muscles steady your trunk while your arms and legs move. They help you lift, carry groceries, climb stairs, change direction, get out of bed and keep your balance.

Core strength isn’t one muscle or one shape. During a one-handed suitcase carry, your trunk stops you leaning sideways. During a push-up, it helps your ribs, pelvis and legs move as one piece. During a step, it passes force between your upper and lower body.
Pick one task you want to support. “Carry two grocery bags without leaning” gives your training a clearer purpose than “get a stronger core.”
Decide whether the task asks you to resist bending, resist twisting, pass force, balance or change position.

items.title: “Core training means doing abdominal crunches.”
items.text: Crunches train one movement. A complete plan also practises resisting movement, carrying, breathing, balance and passing force.

blocks.text: Choose your practical target
Finish this sentence: “I want my core to support me while I ___.”

Breathing changes the pressure and muscle activity around your trunk. Start in a comfortable position. Breathe in without forcing your belly out or lifting your shoulders. Breathe out slowly and notice your belly muscles gently switching on.
A brace is a controlled tightening of your trunk for a task. Imagine getting ready to move a moderately heavy box, not bracing for a surprise snowbank. The tension should match the job.

Practise breathing while keeping light tension. If you have to hold your breath during an easy exercise, make it easier. Some heavy lifting uses deliberate breath-holding, but that needs good coaching and may not suit people with certain health concerns, such as high blood pressure.
Walking needs less bracing than a heavy lift. More tension isn’t always better.

sections.title: Start With Control You Can Repeat

blocks.text: Use a stable position and a small challenge. A heel slide, supported dead bug, bridge, bird dog or plank against a counter can teach your trunk to stay steady while an arm or leg moves.

Choose a version that lets you breathe normally and hold steady. Move slowly. Stop the set when your back arches or presses down hard, your pelvis twists, your shoulders creep up or your breathing gets strained.
The exercise doesn’t need to cause shaking worthy of a weather alert. A clean rep tells you more than a dramatic one.

items.title: “If the exercise burns, the form must be working.”
items.text: You can feel effort with good or poor form. Judge each rep by your breathing, control, symptoms and whether your chosen task improves.

blocks.text: Your trunk handles force from several directions. Some exercises stop too much arching (planks, dead bugs). Some stop twisting (bird dogs, band press-outs). Some stop leaning sideways (side planks, one-handed carries). Controlled bending, arching and turning can also belong in a good plan.

You don’t need an exercise for every angle in one session. Pick two that match your goal. A supported dead bug and a one-handed carry may suit general lifting. A bird dog and a band press-out may suit twisting control. A side plank from the knees is a simple way to start training the sides.
Use positions that fit your body and experience. Kneeling, standing, seated, wall-supported or raised options can replace floor work.
Add one new direction while keeping the setup familiar.

sections.title: Progress the Challenge, Not the Discomfort

blocks.text: You can progress with a longer lever, less hand support, a slightly heavier load, a longer carry, a more upright position or a harder arm or leg movement. Change one thing and stop with several good reps left in reserve.
More time isn’t always better. Several short holds of about 10 seconds, with steady breathing, often train better than one long hold that turns into survival paperwork.

Write down the version, reps or time, and how your target task feels. Mild muscle effort is expected. Sharp, spreading or worsening pain, numbness, weakness, pelvic pressure or a new bulge needs a different response and may need a professional’s check.

items.title: “A stronger core prevents every episode of back pain.”
items.text: Back pain has many possible causes. Core training may help you function, but it can’t guarantee you’ll never have back pain or replace a proper assessment.

sections.title: Andre Builds Strength for the Laundry Stairs

blocks.text: Andre builds strength for the laundry stairs
paragraphs: Andre, 41, lived in a Halifax duplex with the laundry in the basement. He wanted to carry a full basket down the stairs without wobbling, so he had been holding long planks, since they showed up on every exercise list he found online. His plank time improved. The basket stayed unimpressed.

One Sunday, he caught himself leaning hard to one side halfway down the stairs, with no free hand for the railing. It frightened him. He could keep adding plank time, or he could investigate what the staircase was demanding of his body. He booked a session with a trainer at his rec centre.

They tested the real task with a light basket and the railing in reach. Andre leaned and rushed when the basket blocked his view of his feet. The trainer had him practise controlled step-downs, carries with a load at one side and a standing band press-out. She also told him to split big loads while he learned.
Twice a week, he progressed one thing: a little more weight, one more step or less lean to the side. He kept the railing in reach and never practised on the stairs when he was tired.

In week four, he felt strong and tried a full basket on a busy evening. He noticed himself rushing, stopped, set the basket down on the landing, divided the laundry into two smaller loads and made two separate trips. It was the right call.
After six weeks, Andre carried a full basket down the stairs with steady steps and a hand free for the rail. The plank wasn’t useless. It just needed coworkers.

blocks.text: A floor drill builds a skill. A carry, step, reach or lift teaches that skill where life uses it.
Train your core for the task, and the task gets easier.
blocks.detail: Practising the real movement, with one change at a time, builds control you can count on when it matters.
blocks.extra: Section 08 shows how to build a short core sequence into your workouts.

blocks.text: Start with one breathing-and-bracing practice. Add one controlled arm or leg move and one standing or carrying task. Two or three focused exercises fit easily into a full-body workout.

Train the whole body too. Squats, hinges, pushes, pulls, steps and carries already ask your core to work. Separate core exercises can target a specific need, but they don’t need to take over your calendar.
Allow for recovery, and repeat the same sequence long enough to learn it. Variety helps when it solves a problem, not when your routine becomes a weekly scavenger hunt.

Exercise can feel challenging, but it should stay controlled. Stop for sharp pain, worsening back or pelvic symptoms, numbness, weakness that keeps getting worse, dizziness, unusual shortness of breath, pelvic heaviness, leaking urine that worries you or a new bulge in your belly. Get a qualified check when symptoms last or affect your daily life.
This section has no humour on purpose. Symptoms involving nerves, pelvic health, recent surgery or significant pain deserve clear guidance.

items.title: “Everyone should flatten the lower back during every core exercise.”
items.text: The right spine position depends on the exercise, your body, your goal and any professional advice. The useful position is controlled, comfortable and right for the task.

blocks.text: Write down both the drill and the daily task it’s meant to support.

Help with core training may be available from CSEP professionals, physiotherapists, kinesiologists, rec centres, community health programs, pelvic-health physiotherapy, campuses, Indigenous health organizations and adapted exercise services. Coverage, referrals, regulation, eligibility and wait times vary by province and territory.

A physiotherapist can assess pain and movement problems. A pelvic-health physiotherapist can help with pelvic-floor or belly concerns, including after pregnancy. An occupational therapist can help adapt daily tasks and spaces.
Key takeaway

Core strength is the ability to control and pass force through your trunk for a real task. Coordinate your breathing, train more than one direction, progress one thing at a time and connect your drills to standing movement.
Rest a light object on your lower ribs during an easy floor drill. If it keeps launching toward the next postal code, shrink the range and regain control.

items.title: What body regions contribute to the core?
items.detail: Muscles around the abdomen, sides, back, pelvis, hips, and breathing system.

items.title: What is a brace?
items.detail: A controlled increase in trunk tension matched to a task.

items.title: Why should breathing continue during an easy core exercise?
items.detail: It shows that the challenge permits control and avoids unnecessary strain.

items.title: Name two force directions the trunk may manage.
items.detail: Extension, rotation, side-bending, flexion, or force transfer.

items.title: Give two ways to progress a core exercise.
items.detail: Use a longer lever, less support, more load, a longer carry, or a more complex movement.

items.title: Why did Andre change his plan?
items.detail: His long planks improved, but they did not adequately practise the loaded stair task.

items.title: Why should core work connect to whole-body training?
items.detail: Daily movement requires the trunk to coordinate with the arms, legs, balance, and breathing.

items.title: Name two symptoms that mean stop or seek assessment.
items.detail: Sharp or worsening pain, numbness, weakness, dizziness, pelvic heaviness, concerning leakage, or a new bulge.

blocks.text: Complete the relevant safety screen. Choose one daily task, one controlled core drill, and one standing or carrying exercise. Practise them twice this week, then retest the task without forcing through symptoms.
Skip any medical details or symptoms in this form. Just the plan.

items.title: Anti-extension
items.text: Resisting a force that would excessively arch the trunk.

items.title: Anti-rotation
items.text: Resisting a force that would turn the trunk.

items.title: Brace
items.text: Controlled trunk tension used to support a movement or load.

items.title: Core
items.text: Muscles and related structures that help control the trunk, pelvis, and force transfer.

items.title: Force transfer
items.text: Moving or managing force between body regions during a task.
